Quantile normalization here means an affine rescaling based on fixed percentiles of the training data.
It changes the numerical coordinates used by a model, such as the coordinates of a robot action.
Start with the [representation overview](../machine-learning/representations.qmd); compare [activation normalization](../machine-learning/normalization.qmd#what-to-check-when-reading-a-model) for transformations inside a network.

## Quantile scaling changes coordinates {#quantile-scaling}

For coordinate $j$, let $l_j$ and $u_j$ be its first and ninety-ninth percentiles, estimated from the training data.
These are fixed reference values, rather than statistics recomputed from each incoming action chunk.
The quantile scaling used by [FAST, §V-B](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.09747), maps these reference points to approximately $-1$ and $1$.
Writing $r_j=u_j-l_j+\epsilon$ with a small positive numerical stabiliser,

$$
  \tilde x_j=2\frac{x_j-l_j}{r_j}-1.
$$

The [OpenPI implementation](https://github.com/Physical-Intelligence/openpi/blob/main/src/openpi/transforms.py) uses $\epsilon=10^{-6}$ and applies no clipping in this operation.
The lower reference maps exactly to $-1$; the upper maps approximately to $1$ because of $\epsilon$.
Values beyond the reference interval can remain outside $[-1,1]$.
Percentiles reduce the influence of extreme samples on the chosen scale; they do not delete those samples.

For nonconstant coordinates, this is an affine change of coordinates: differences are multiplied by the same fixed factor.
It does not turn a multimodal distribution into a Gaussian.
A rank-based Gaussian transform instead applies an estimated cumulative distribution function followed by the inverse Gaussian cumulative distribution function, $\Phi^{-1}(\widehat F(x))$.
That nonlinear operation changes relative spacings between values.

Different robot coordinates need separate statistics because their units and operating ranges differ.
Scaling also changes the relative weight assigned by [squared loss](../machine-learning/loss.qmd#mse): a fixed physical error receives a larger normalised penalty when its reference range is smaller.
Comparable numerical ranges do not establish comparable physical importance.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: inversion and the weighting of errors"}

Rearranging the affine map gives

$$
  x_j=\frac{\tilde x_j+1}{2}r_j+l_j.
$$

For a prediction $\hat x_j$ and target $x_j$ transformed with identical statistics,

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \hat{\tilde x}_j-\tilde x_j
  &=\frac{2}{r_j}(\hat x_j-x_j),\\
  (\hat{\tilde x}_j-\tilde x_j)^2
  &=\frac{4}{r_j^2}(\hat x_j-x_j)^2.
  \end{aligned}
$$

Ignoring the tiny stabiliser, reference values $l=-2$ and $u=6$ send $x=2$ to $0$ and $x=10$ to $2$.
The inverse maps $0$ back to $2$.
If a separate operation clips $2$ to $1$, inversion returns $6$, so the original $10$ cannot be recovered.
Clipping is many-to-one; the unclipped affine map is invertible.

:::

Deployment must use the statistics and coordinate conventions associated with training.
Re-estimating them from the current scene changes what the same model output means physically.
For example, normalised zero denotes the midpoint of the chosen reference interval, not necessarily zero joint angle or zero velocity.
Inverting normalisation also does not undo unrelated transformations such as converting absolute targets into displacements; each transformation needs its own inverse.
